strengths: Novel problem formulation: First to seriously address lifelong head avatar modeling from psychology/identity perspective, establishing new research direction with clear motivation
Comprehensive technical execution: Neural parametric model elegantly extends 3DMM principles; Dynamo's dynamic basis pruning is clever; DNA-2DGS design well-motivated for rendering and meshing
Extensive experimental validation: Multiple evaluation protocols, 8+ baseline comparisons, ablation studies, identity consistency metrics, and cross-dataset evaluation (INSTA + TimeWalker-1.0)
Strong quantitative results: Outperforms baselines on primary metrics (PSNR 27.28, SSIM 0.949, LPIPS 0.071); demonstrates successful cross-lifestage/cross-identity reenactment and mesh reconstruction
Substantial dataset contribution: TimeWalker-1.0 with 40 identities, 2.7M frames, diverse attributes (age 20-80, ethnicities, accessories) fills gap in lifelong avatar datasets
Transparent limitations and ethical considerations: Honest discussion of FLAME constraints, view angle limitations, data imbalance; includes ethics statement and data usage agreements
weaknesses: Oversold 'lifelong' framing: Limited to ages 20-80 (not true infancy-to-old-age), celebrities only with curated data; paper positions as 'preliminary exploration' but marketing emphasizes 'lifelong' throughout

Fundamental FLAME dependency: Architecture tightly coupled to FLAME's fixed topology; exaggerated expressions and unseen parts cause visible artifacts; directly limits the claimed 'full-scale animation' capability

Critical view synthesis limitations: Noticeable degradation beyond 45° yaw angle (Fig. 12); this range is restrictive for practical applications (telepresence, archiving); root cause (data distribution) acknowledged but unsolved

Imperfect disentanglement: Lighting separation via residual embeddings shows identity drift and artifacts (Section F.4); authors acknowledge 'disentanglement not yet perfect,' undermining claims of steerable space

Limited generalization: Method is person-specific requiring retraining per identity; celebrities only; data augmentation with large models showed mixed results; scalability to general populations unclear

Experimental fairness concerns: Protocol-2 comparison uses single model (ours) vs. N models (baselines) for N lifestages; GAGAvatar/GPHM comparisons limited (not open-sourced); PAV reimplemented by authors

Insufficient design justification: Dynamo threshold κ selection heuristic; loss weight tuning procedure undocumented; why 2DGS over dynamic 3DGS beyond depth handling not justified; warm-up phase impact unquantified

Narrow experimental scope: Only 5 identities in main experiments; more results in appendix but limited diversity; no user perceptual studies; computational costs (3-5hrs training, 10min/mesh) not addressed for scalability

Incomplete large-scale pretraining exploration: Section I.1 on combining with large models feels preliminary; post-processing and data augmentation attempts yielded limited benefits, suggesting underdeveloped direction

strengths: Novel problem formulation shifting from momentary to lifelong avatar modeling, well-motivated by psychology/sociology perspectives and opening a new research direction
Principled technical design combining classical 3DMM principles with neural representations; Dynamo module intelligently discovers minimal basis set rather than memorizing independent snapshots

Comprehensive experimental evaluation with two evaluation protocols, 8 baselines, thorough ablations, and multiple evaluation metrics (rendering quality, mesh reconstruction, identity consistency, viewpoint robustness)
Valuable dataset contribution (TimeWalker-1.0) with 40 celebrities, 2.7M frames, diverse ages 20-80, and comprehensive attribute statistics providing a benchmark for future lifelong modeling research
Honest and thorough discussion of limitations (FLAME constraints, exaggerated expressions, data noise) strengthening paper credibility and identifying clear directions for future work
Strong reproducibility support with detailed hyperparameters, training procedures, loss formulations, and promised open-source release
Solid technical execution with sound mathematical formulation and experimental design supporting the main claims
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in individual components: Gaussian Surfels [19], multi-resolution hashgrids [51], FLAME inverse warping [90] are from prior work; Dynamo's threshold-based pruning is straightforward; contribution is primarily in combination rather than novel algorithms

Critical dependency on FLAME template limits applicability: fixed topology causes artifacts with exaggerated expressions and unseen parts (tongue); FLAME fitting quality degrades on in-the-wild data introducing preprocessing errors; fundamentally constrains scope to standard head expressions

Insufficient theoretical justification: limited analysis of why linear combination works specifically for lifelong modeling beyond 3DMM precedent; no theoretical guarantees that Dynamo learns meaningful vs. spurious features; loose connection between identity formation psychology theory and technical design

Incomplete lifelong scope: age range only 20-80 (no childhood/adolescence); aging captures primarily appearance (texture/wrinkles) not structural geometric changes; dataset biased toward celebrities with extensive internet documentation; 'lifelong' framing overstates actual coverage

Experimental setup concerns: Protocol 1 comparison (single unified model vs. multiple baseline models per lifestage) structurally favors proposed method; limited quantitative comparison with most relevant baseline (PAV [9]) in main paper; identity consistency only compared with one baseline; main results on only 5/40 identities

Underdeveloped data sparsity claims: 500-3000 frames per lifestage is not particularly sparse; Table 4 shows modest multi-lifestage improvements (27.22 vs 23.69 PSNR); unclear if added complexity justified over independent momentary models

Missing critical ablations: no sensitivity analysis for multiple manual loss weights (Table 6); no computational cost comparison with baselines; limited analysis of what each Dynamo basis captures; insufficient justification for architectural choices (e.g., why multi-resolution hashgrids)

Practical applicability concerns: requires substantial per-person unstructured data collection; FLAME constraints limit expressivity; unclear if lifelong modeling is preferable to simpler alternatives like momentary reconstruction plus temporal interpolation; large-viewpoint rendering degrades significantly beyond 45 degrees
